title: Section 1 · The image classification task
caption: Start with the dataset, choose an image label, then ask which parts of the photograph help us decide.
notes:
What should a model predict from a photograph?
Pause at the section question. Connect the previous result to the three steps, then advance to the concrete example.

title: What does our animal dataset look like?
caption: Oxford-IIIT Pet: six examples. Each photo has a species label and a breed label.
notes:
What changes across photos that share the same dog or cat label?
Point to pose, coat and background. Read the species label first, then the breed beneath it.

title: How many images and classes are there?
caption: Our opening question uses 2 classes: cat or dog. Predicting the breed would use 37 classes.
notes:
Could the same photograph have a two-class target in one task and a 37-class target in another?
Point back to the two labels under each photo. Add the two split sizes to recover the total.

title: What shape is one image?
caption: Original sizes vary. Our demo uses 224 × 224 pixels, each with red, green and blue values: 150,528 numbers.
notes:
What does each of the three dimensions count?
Trace the original photograph to the exact model crop. Multiply height by width by the three RGB channels.

title: What animal do you see?
caption: Which parts of the photograph helped you decide?
notes:
What animal is this, and which parts made you decide?
Point to the face, fur, and silhouette before mentioning an architecture.

title: Classification: name the animal
caption: Output: one class label for each photograph. Our example labels are dog and cat.
notes:
What would you want the program to return for each photo?
Reveal dog and cat. Connect one image label to the spam/not-spam example in Part I.

title: Our task today: classify the whole image
caption: For the rest of this lecture, we observe the whole photograph and predict one class label.
notes:
Are we trying to guess a missing patch in this task?
Point to the full observed image and the two possible class labels.

title: What were we asking the text model to predict?
caption: A name grows one character at a time. Our fixed-window model scores the possible next characters.
notes:
After predicting one letter, how would we generate a whole name?
Follow the loop back to the input, now with one more token.

title: And what were we predicting in the bank example?
caption: Here one token is a word. The final “the” row uses the earlier context to predict what comes next; “water” is one plausible continuation.
notes:
Which row predicts the word after this whole prefix: bank, or the final the?
Read the familiar sentence. Point to the final the, follow its updated row to the word scores, then reveal water as a possible continuation.

title: What changed, and what stayed the same?
caption: Both models score possible answers. What they observe, summarize and predict differs.
notes:
Which parts of our old calculation can we reuse unchanged?
Compare one row at a time. Refer back to the image summary from the classification slide; its construction comes later.

title: Would you recognize this crop on its own?
caption: Fur, shadow, or background? Seeing the face elsewhere in the photo helps us interpret this crop.
notes:
Could this dark crop be fur, a shadow, or something else?
Connect to the previous slide: we still predict one label for the whole image. Reveal the crop’s location, then point to the face. Introduce attention as the way patch representations will use context; the following slides explain how.

title: What can we carry over from our text models?
caption: We still turn inputs into rows, read useful information, and predict an answer.
notes:
What stays the same when the input is a photograph?
Point to representation, contextual reading, and multiple head messages in the earlier examples.

title: What can the face tell this dark patch?
caption: We want one image label. Face context can help interpret the dark texture and make its patch representation more useful for that prediction.
notes:
Could nearby face information help us interpret the dark texture as animal fur?
Start at the dark receiver. Reveal the face source, then trace its information box all the way to the receiver’s numbers.

title: Should every source contribute equally?
caption: Here, face clues could help more than branches. Attention weights control how much each source contributes to the message.
notes:
For this dark receiver, which source would you expect to be more useful: the face or the branches?
Keep the receiver fixed. Reveal the second source, then compare the thick and thin arrows ending on the same receiver row.

title: What changes when the patch gets context?
caption: Attention supplies a weighted message. The block adds it to the patch row; later layers use the updated rows to predict one image label.
notes:
Are we changing the photo, assigning a fur label to this crop, or updating its numerical representation?
Point to the unchanged pixels, then follow the current row and context message into the plus sign. End at the updated row.

title: Back to text: what did attention update?
caption: Each token starts with an embedding plus position. Attention supplies context; adding its update gives a new representation of the same token.
notes:
Did attention replace the word bank, or change the numbers representing it?
Trace bank through the middle row. Then point to the final the: that is the row used to predict the next word after this full prefix.

title: What could be the image equivalent of a token?
caption: We can use one fixed-size patch as an image token. Each patch gets its own row, just as each text token did.
notes:
Should one image token be a pixel, an object, or a fixed-size piece of the image?
Pause on the whole photo. Reveal the grid, then follow the outlined patch to the idea of one token row.

title: What could be the image equivalent of an embedding?
caption: Text uses a learned lookup table. A patch projection produces D coordinates per patch. D is shared across patches and can differ from the number of pixel values.
notes:
Where would a vector for this crop come from, if we have no word ID to look up?
Read the actual bank embedding from Part II. Keep the image row unrevealed while students suggest how pixels could become numbers.

title: What could a query be in the image?
caption: The row being updated makes a query. Its learned projection determines what kinds of source information it can match.
notes:
Which patch should make the query if we want to update the dark patch?
Follow the receiver row through W_Q in each case. Read the questions as intuition for a learned vector, not words typed by a user.

title: Could this dark texture belong to the animal?
caption: Face and coat clues could help this patch represent part of the animal. The classifier will still predict one label for the whole photo.
notes:
What is missing from this crop, and which other crop could help interpret it?
Locate the purple receiver in the photograph. Reveal its possible question, then inspect the two source crops before showing the projection.

title: Where is the rest of this face?
caption: One patch contains only part of a face. Context from other patches could help its representation describe a larger visual structure.
notes:
What is missing from this crop, and which other crop could help interpret it?
Locate the purple receiver in the photograph. Reveal its possible question, then inspect the two source crops before showing the projection.

title: Where does this branch continue?
caption: Background patches can also gather context. A branch representation could use nearby edge continuity; the task still predicts the image label.
notes:
What is missing from this crop, and which other crop could help interpret it?
Locate the purple receiver in the photograph. Reveal its possible question, then inspect the two source crops before showing the projection.

title: What could a key be in the image?
caption: Each source row makes a key. Comparing the receiver’s query with source keys gives the scores used to choose attention weights.
notes:
How could the dark patch compare a face patch with a branches patch?
Keep the query on the receiver. Point to river and the face as sources, each with its own key.

title: What could each source offer for matching?
caption: A source key can match one query well and another poorly. Comparing this receiver’s query with all source keys sets its attention weights.
notes:
Could the branch key be useful to the branch receiver even if the dark receiver gives it little weight?
Hold the dark query fixed and compare the three source keys. Then recall the branch query: a key’s relevance depends on the query.

title: What information would a value send?
caption: Q and K choose the weights. V supplies the information to combine using those weights; the combined message updates the receiving representation.
notes:
Once a source receives a weight, which vector actually contributes to the message?
Reuse the same source crops from the key slide. Replace W_K with W_V, then multiply each value by its weight.

title: What information could these values carry?
caption: Each source supplies one value vector. Different receivers mix these values with different weights. Here a₁₀,₇ is the weight for P10 reading P7.
notes:
If two receivers read the same source, does the source need a new value vector for each receiver?
Keep the source crops fixed from the key slide. Follow W_V into the value vectors, then reveal the weighted sum; the dots include the other sources.

title: What is the “next token” for this image?
caption: Here the target is an image label. We reuse attention to build representations; our classification task changes what we read out and predict.
notes:
Are we predicting another patch, another word, or one label for this photograph?
Pause before revealing the image answer. Contrast vocabulary scores with class scores, then return to how the patch rows are built.

title: How can we give this photograph to attention?
caption: Attention works on rows of numbers. Next, we choose image patches and turn their pixels into those rows.
notes:
In the text lessons, what did attention receive as its input?
Keep the photograph visible. Reveal its pieces, one row per piece, then the familiar attention operation.

title: Section 2 · From pixels to patch embeddings
caption: Read one small patch, calculate its embedding, then scale the same operation to a real photograph.
notes:
How do we make those rows from an image?
Pause at the section question. Connect the previous result to the three steps, then advance to the concrete example.

title: The whole route: photograph to prediction
caption: First turn pixels into patch features. Prepare those rows, let them exchange information, then read one image summary to score the classes. We will open each box as we reach it.
notes:
Where do pixels become features, and where do features become class scores?
Trace left to right. For now, call the extra row an image summary. Explain its name and how it works in the dedicated detour before attention.

title: Where do the patch boundaries go?
caption: The grid cuts through the photograph before the model knows where the dog is.
notes:
Does each patch contain one whole object?
Reveal the grid, then match each enlarged crop back to its location.

title: How can a red pixel be three numbers?
caption: Each pixel records a red, green and blue channel.
notes:
What would [0,0,0] look like?
Name the channels, then ask for black, red and white before revealing the rows.

title: Read the RGB values of each pixel
caption: For this calculation, divide RGB values by 255. Read A, B, C, D: top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right.
notes:
How many numbers does pixel A contribute?
Point to the red pixel, read its RGB triple, then reveal one pixel at a time.

title: Put the four RGB triples in one row
caption: Keep RGB together for each pixel. x₁ contains 12 values from patch 1; the subscript identifies the patch.
notes:
Which three entries came from the bottom-right pixel?
Follow A, B, C and D into their matching groups, then count the twelve scalar entries.

title: Which pixel goes first in the row?
caption: Read left to right, then return to the start of the next row. The 0s and 1s are pixel values, not step numbers.
notes:
After the top-right pixel, which pixel should we read next?
Trace the blue arrow across the top row, around to bottom-left, and across the bottom row. Then match those values to the output row.

title: How does this connect to text embeddings?
caption: Here the patch embedding is x₁W + b, with no activation afterward. Text looks up a learned row; the image layer computes one from pixels.
notes:
Do we have a vocabulary ID for every possible image patch?
Compare lookup on the left with computation on the right. Keep the number of input values separate from the embedding width.

title: Do we apply an activation after the patch layer?
caption: Our patch embedding uses one affine layer. The later block MLP puts GELU between two linear layers. D is the embedding width; H is the MLP’s hidden width.
notes:
Which part of these two paths applies an activation function?
Follow the direct pixel-to-embedding path first. Then reveal the separate block MLP and point to GELU between its two linear layers.

title: What does “projection” mean here?
caption: A projection forms weighted sums of the pixel values and adds a bias. This one linear layer turns 12 inputs into a 2-coordinate patch embedding.
notes:
How many weighted sums do we need to produce two output coordinates?
Match 12 to in_features and 2 to out_features, then follow the matrix dimensions.

title: 12 input numbers, 2 output numbers
caption: Each input node holds one RGB value. Both outputs read all 12 inputs. Together, y₁ and y₂ form the embedding for this one patch.
notes:
How many connections enter each output node?
Count the twelve actual pixel values. Follow their connections into each of the two outputs, then reveal the weights and biases.

title: Follow the connections into output 1
caption: Multiply each input by its connection weight, add the contributions, then add the bias. The highlighted connections show the nonzero weights for this output.
notes:
What does this output receive before we add its bias?
Reveal the highlighted edges and their weights. Read the connected input values, compute the sum, then add the bias and reveal the answer.

title: Now follow the connections into output 2
caption: Multiply each input by its connection weight, add the contributions, then add the bias. The highlighted connections show the nonzero weights for this output.
notes:
What does this output receive before we add its bias?
Reveal the highlighted edges and their weights. Read the connected input values, compute the sum, then add the bias and reveal the answer.

title: These two numbers are the patch embedding
caption: c₁ represents the content of patch 1. Its two coordinates are features for the model; the image classifier comes later.
notes:
Should the negative output become zero?
Collect the two calculated coordinates and point to the absence of an activation after the layer.

title: Apply the very same layer to another patch
caption: The pixel rows differ. Both use the same 26 parameters, so we compute both embeddings with one call: C = proj(X).
notes:
Do we create a new nn.Linear layer when we move to patch 2?
Reveal the second patch. Follow both arrows through the single weight-and-bias box, then read the stacked input and output shapes.

title: Start with the same dog photograph
caption: We now carry this one image through the real model’s input pipeline. It has already been resized and cropped to 224 × 224 RGB pixels.
notes:
What do the three image dimensions count?
Keep the photograph fixed. Identify rows, columns and RGB channels before introducing any patch or embedding dimension.

title: Split the image into 16 × 16 patches
caption: The x-axis runs right; the y-axis runs down. Both span 224 pixels. Cut every 16 pixels along each axis. Each piece keeps its RGB values; we will count the pieces next.
notes:
How many 16-pixel-wide pieces fit along each image axis?
Point to the x-axis arrow, then the y-axis arrow and their endpoints. Follow the highlighted image region into the enlarged 16×16 patch. Leave the count for the next slide.

title: Number the patches row by row
caption: Number left to right, then continue on the next row. Use the image and patch sizes to calculate the row length and total before revealing the answers.
notes:
What is the last patch number in the first row? What starts the second row, and what is the final patch number?
Start with P1 and P2. Ask students to divide each 224-pixel extent by 16, then reveal P14 and the second row. Multiply the two counts before revealing P196 and the full array shape.

title: Read the RGB values inside patch 63
caption: P63 contains 256 pixels. Its first pixel is RGB [16, 17, 12]; its next pixel is [41, 42, 37]. Three values per pixel give 768 numbers in this same patch.
notes:
How many input numbers does each pixel contribute?
Use the two outlined pixels in the real crop. Read each RGB triple, then count 256 triples rather than introducing 768 without its source.

title: Normalize those same RGB values
caption: The checkpoint rescales every channel using the same formula. For the first red value, (16 / 255 − 0.5) / 0.5 ≈ −0.875. P63 still contains 768 values.
notes:
Where does the first negative number come from?
Carry the first RGB triple from the previous slide across the arrow. Work out the red channel before revealing the second pixel.

title: Flatten patch 63 into one row
caption: Copy the normalized RGB triples in pixel order: first pixel, second pixel, and so on. This gives x₆₃ with shape 1 × 768. The subscript 63 identifies the patch.
notes:
Which three entries came from the second pixel?
Follow the scan arrow across the patch, then point to the two corresponding triples in the row. Keep the same values visible across the transition.

title: Pass that row through the shared linear layer
caption: This layer reads 768 values and computes 192 output features. Its learned weights and biases are shared by every patch. One patch row enters; one embedding row leaves.
notes:
How many weighted sums does this layer compute for P63?
Carry x63 from the previous slide into the layer. Follow its row count and feature width separately, then identify the weight and bias shapes.

title: Read the 192 output features for patch 63
caption: The layer produces c₆₃, the content embedding for P63. These are actual outputs from the pretrained model, rounded here. The first feature is −0.852 and the last is −1.199.
notes:
Which patch do all 192 numbers describe?
Trace the same crop through the same layer, then read individual output coordinates before collecting them into c63.

title: Pass patch 64 through the very same layer
caption: P64 is the patch immediately to the right of P63. Its different pixels give a different embedding. Both patches use the same weights and biases, and both produce 192 output features.
notes:
Do we create new projection weights for P64?
Keep P63’s path visible while revealing P64 underneath it. Point to the one shared layer and compare their measured input and output values.

title: Stack the 196 output rows into C
caption: Repeat the same projection for all 196 patches and keep their order. The input matrix X is 196 × 768. The output matrix C is 196 × 192: one content embedding per image patch.
notes:
Which axis changes when we apply the shared projection to all patches?
Match the illustrated crops to their measured output rows. Then carry the unchanged row count 196 from X through the layer to C.

title: Section 3 · Prepare the rows, then classify the image
caption: Keep the photograph fixed. Give each patch its location, introduce the summary row, then follow the complete input through the classifier.
notes:
Where is each patch? How do we get one image summary?
Pause at the section question. Connect the previous result to the three steps, then advance to the concrete example.

title: Give each patch its location in the photograph
caption: Recognizing a face depends on how its parts are arranged. c₆₃ describes this crop; p₆₃ tells attention where it belongs. Add them so the model can use both appearance and layout.
notes:
Which part of the shared patch projection received row 5, column 7?
None: the projection received only pixel values. Point to the location on the unchanged photograph, then introduce its position vector.

title: Add position to these content rows
caption: c₆₃ comes from the patch pixels. p₆₃ is learned for its grid location. Add matching coordinates to get e₆₃. All three rows have 192 coordinates; addition does not double the width.
notes:
After adding position, does this row have 192 coordinates or 384?
Keep the crop visible. Recall the projection that made c63, then add its learned position row coordinate by coordinate to make e63.

title: CLS: one summary for the whole image
caption: Before we enter attention, decide where the image summary will live. This model reserves one extra row called CLS, short for classification token. Then we return to the same forward pass.
notes:
We have 196 descriptions. Which representation should the classifier read?
Pause the computation. Explain the need for one image summary before introducing an extra row of numbers.

title: Add a summary row beside the dog’s patch rows
caption: A patch row comes from pixels. CLS comes from a separate set of model parameters. No extra crop is cut from the photograph. Its 192 coordinates match the width of every patch row.
notes:
Where are the pixels for CLS?
There are none. Trace the two different origins: a crop through the patch layer, and a separately stored parameter row.

title: Create 192 trainable numbers for CLS
caption: Before training, initialize one 192-number vector. It is stored in the model, like a learned token embedding in text. The numbers do not come from this photograph. Training will adjust them.
notes:
Why 192, and who supplies the initial numbers?
The chosen embedding width is 192. The initialization routine supplies the numbers once, before training; no image pixels are needed.

title: The image label teaches the starting CLS numbers
caption: The label supplies a loss on the prediction. Backpropagation reaches the starting CLS vector through the classifier and blocks. The optimizer adjusts its 192 parameters, along with other trainable weights, across many labelled images.
notes:
Do we need 192 target numbers for CLS?
No. The image’s class label provides the loss; the chain rule supplies gradients for the starting vector.

title: Load the learned CLS for our dog example
caption: The saved model already contains the learned CLS vector and its position vector. Add them to form its starting input row. Load these same parameters for every photograph; no pixel values are needed for this row.
notes:
Are these numbers freshly sampled for this photograph?
No. They are saved trained parameters. Add the CLS position vector, then combine this row with the dog’s patch rows.

title: The dog’s patches turn CLS into this image’s summary
caption: The dog’s patch rows bring the image information. Attention lets CLS gather it, and the blocks update its features. Read the final CLS to predict Newfoundland. The stored starting parameters stay fixed during this forward pass.
notes:
Which numbers change while we classify this photo?
The CLS activation changes through the blocks; the stored parameter does not. Point to the dog’s patch rows as the source of image-specific information.

title: The same CLS start reads two different photographs
caption: Both images use the same starting CLS and the same model parameters. Their patch rows differ, so attention produces different updates. These are measured CLS values after the first attention update and residual addition.
notes:
The starting numbers match exactly. Why do the two outputs differ?
Point to the different photos. Their patches supply different keys and values. The starting CLS query is the same; the resulting attention message can differ.

title: Read the two final summaries to classify the photographs
caption: After all 12 blocks and final normalization, the two CLS representations differ. The same classifier reads each 192-number summary. It predicts Newfoundland for this dog and Persian cat for this cat.
notes:
Did we learn separate CLS parameters for these two photos?
No. One shared starting parameter led to two image-dependent activations. The class head also uses the same weights for both images.

title: With CLS, read the dog’s final summary row
caption: The dog supplies 196 patch rows. Add the shared CLS row, update all 197 rows through the blocks, then read the final CLS. Its 192 features produce the saved Newfoundland prediction.
notes:
Which row does the classifier read, and how did the dog enter that row?
Follow the purple CLS row. Attention mixes information from the dog’s patch rows into it. The blocks update patch rows too.

title: Without CLS, combine the dog’s final patch rows
caption: Build a second design with 196 patch rows and no CLS. Attention still lets the patches share information. Average their final features to get one 192-number summary. Train the classifier and blocks with this readout.
notes:
Without an extra summary row, where is the information about this dog?
It remains in the 196 contextual patch representations. Average corresponding coordinates across these rows, then classify the resulting vector.

title: Mean pooling: average each feature across the patches
caption: Each row is a patch representation after it has read context. Average feature 1 across patches, then feature 2. Four rows become one row. In the full model, 196 rows become one 192-feature summary.
notes:
Does pooling average the pixels, or the features after attention?
The final features. Ask students to compute each column average. Each feature coordinate is retained; only the patch axis is reduced.

title: Both choices give one summary for the dog photograph
caption: Both designs can learn image classification. Train for the chosen readout: removing CLS from our saved model changes its computation. We will continue with its CLS route, whose dog prediction we have already followed.
notes:
Is CLS required for image classification? Can we delete it from our saved model and expect the same answer?
It is not required as an architectural choice. But a model trained to read CLS has learned that route; changing it calls for adaptation and evaluation.

title: Add the summary row: 196 + 1 = 197
caption: Each patch keeps its content-plus-position row. CLS gets its own learned position too. Stack the summary and patch rows into E: 197 rows, each with 192 features. Batch size one is omitted here.
notes:
Why do we now have 197 rows, while the width is still 192?
Identify the extra row at the top. Position is added coordinate by coordinate. The subscript is the row’s identity, not its width.

title: Start with one Transformer block
caption: Our 196 patch rows and one CLS row enter block 1. Attention shares information across rows; the MLP transforms each row. The output still has 197 rows and 192 features per row.
notes:
What goes into one block, and what comes out?
Keep the scope to block 1. Follow prepared rows through attention and then the MLP. Same matrix shape, updated feature values. Explain the stack only after these operations.

title: Make queries, keys and values from these rows
caption: LayerNorm rescales a row’s features and keeps its width. We name it here and study its details later. Three learned maps then make Q, K and V; the diagram shows one of three heads.
notes:
Which projection reads pixels, and which projections read the prepared embedding row?
Trace the small recap first. Enter the block with e63, normalize it, then split into the three separate learned projections for head one.

title: The same input matrix feeds three learned projections
caption: One normalized matrix X feeds three different learned projections. Q, K and V each contain 197 rows of 64 features, in the same token order. This is one head; dots stand for omitted values.
notes:
Do Q, K and V come from three different images?
Trace all three arrows back to the same X. The learned weights differ. Each projection processes every row using the same weights within that projection.

title: One query–key comparison fills one matrix cell
caption: Multiply Q by Kᵀ and divide by √64 = 8. Row CLS, column P63 compares the CLS query with patch 63’s key. Every query–key pair gets a score. These scores are not yet attention weights.
notes:
Which query and which key produced the highlighted cell?
Follow the highlighted row of Q and column of Kᵀ to row CLS, column P63 of S. The dot product sums 64 coordinate products. S can contain negative scores and need not be symmetric.

title: Follow the CLS row from scores to weights
caption: Enlarge the highlighted CLS row. Its 197 scores include CLS itself and all 196 patches. Softmax normalizes this entire row into 197 weights that sum to one. Every image patch is available; no causal mask is needed.
notes:
Are there 196 scores or 197 scores in the highlighted CLS row?
There are 196 patch scores plus the CLS self-score. Reveal the zoom, then the weights. The same query produces every score in this row; only the source key changes. Nothing is hidden behind a causal mask.

title: Turn each query’s 197 scores into 197 source weights
caption: Apply softmax across each score row. The CLS row becomes weights over CLS and all 196 patches, summing to one. Each other query gets its own weight row. These weights tell us how to mix the value rows.
notes:
What are the alternatives in this softmax: animal classes or source rows?
They are sources, including CLS itself. a(CLS,P63) is normalized against all 197 scores in the CLS row. Every row sums to one; columns need not.

title: Every image row can read every image row
caption: Next-token prediction hides later text positions. Here the complete photograph is available before classification. Every query can use every key and value, including itself. The ViT attention matrix has no causal triangle removed.
notes:
If CLS is the first row, what would a causal mask let it read?
Only itself. That would prevent it from gathering patch information. This classifier uses full attention because all image patches are available for the image-label prediction.

title: The dog’s feature rows become value rows
caption: Use the same normalized input X that produced Q and K. The value projection makes 64 features for each of its 197 rows. P63’s crop identifies one source; its value row contains learned features.
notes:
Where does row P63 of V come from?
Follow P63’s normalized 192-feature row through the shared value projection. It produces 64 features. CLS has a value row too, although it has no image crop.

title: One weight scales all 64 features in its value row
caption: P63’s CLS weight multiplies every coordinate of P63’s value row. The result still has 64 features. Repeat for CLS itself and every patch. The numbers shown are rounded from the saved dog computation.
notes:
Does a₆₃ multiply one feature, or all 64 features?
It scales the entire P63 value row. This is one source’s contribution to the CLS message, not the completed message.

title: Add the weighted rows to make one CLS message
caption: Multiply the CLS weight row by V: (1 × 197) × (197 × 64) gives 1 × 64. Each output feature adds 197 weighted contributions. This is the message for one query in one head.
notes:
Why does the result have 64 coordinates, rather than 197?
We sum over sources. Each column of V contributes one feature to the output row. All 64 feature columns remain; each contains a sum over 197 weighted sources.

title: Repeat for every query: H has 197 message rows
caption: Multiply A by V. For CLS, multiply each source value row by its attention weight, then add the 197 weighted rows. The result is one 64-feature message. Do this for every query to form H.
notes:
Where does P63’s information enter the message to CLS?
Match column P63 of A with row P63 of V. Its weight multiplies all 64 coordinates of that source’s value row. Add the contributions from all sources.

title: From one completed head to three parallel heads
caption: We have finished one head’s attention calculation. This model has three heads. Each starts from the same input rows and computes its own messages. Next, follow those parallel paths and combine their outputs before the MLP.
notes:
Have we finished head 1, or already updated the input E?
We have its message matrix H¹. The output projection and residual addition still follow. Introduce the other heads only now; they run alongside head 1 and do not consume its output.

title: The same rows feed three sets of Q, K and V
caption: All three heads read the same normalized matrix X. Each has its own Q, K and V projection weights and biases. Every output matrix has 197 rows and 64 features. The highlighted first row is always CLS.
notes:
Do we create three CLS tokens or divide the patches between the heads?
Neither. Every head reads all 197 rows, including the same 192-feature CLS input. Each applies a different learned projection. Superscripts 1, 2 and 3 name heads.

title: Each head repeats the complete attention calculation
caption: Within each head, compare Q with K, scale the scores, apply softmax across each row, then multiply by that head’s V. Each path returns 197 messages of 64 features. The heads operate in parallel.
notes:
Does head 2 use head 1’s attention weights or its value matrix?
No. Keep each colored path intact: Qʰ and Kʰ produce Aʰ, which mixes Vʰ to make Hʰ. Every head has its own 197×197 weight matrix.

title: One CLS input produces three different messages
caption: CLS is the same input row for all heads. Their learned projections produce different queries, keys and values, so their attention computations produce different messages. These measured messages each contain 64 features. There is still one CLS token.
notes:
What is shared, and what differs, across these three CLS paths?
The normalized CLS input is shared. The projection parameters, projected queries/keys/values, source weights and resulting messages differ. Each message also depends on the patch values and keys from this photograph.

title: Concatenate the three CLS messages
caption: Keep all three messages by placing their coordinates side by side. The joined CLS row has 192 features: 64 from head 1, then 64 from head 2, then 64 from head 3. Concatenation has no learned parameters.
notes:
Does concatenation add corresponding numbers from different heads?
No. Follow each vector into its own feature range. The coordinates retain their values and order. Joining happens across the feature dimension, keeping one receiver row.

title: Keep the embedding; add the context from attention
caption: Follow two paths from E. The heads produce messages; concatenate and project them to make ΔE. The skip path carries E directly to addition. U = E + ΔE is the contextualized representation passed to the MLP.
notes:
Which operation learns to combine the head features, and which row gets the residual update?
Linear(192,192) learns the combination. Add the result to E, before the attention branch’s LayerNorm. The MLP will receive this updated row through its own LayerNorm.

title: The dog’s CLS keeps its input and gains context
caption: Add the projected attention update coordinate by coordinate to the original CLS embedding. This produces a contextualized CLS row of the same width. It continues through the MLP and later blocks before the classifier reads the final summary.
notes:
Is the attention update already the contextualized embedding, or do we still add something?
The update is Δe₀. The contextualized row is u₀=e₀+Δe₀. Add the original block input, before LayerNorm. The 192 output features are a representation; class scores are computed later.

title: Open block 1: attention, then the MLP
caption: One block makes two updates. Attention lets rows exchange information; the MLP transforms each resulting row. Each branch adds its update to its input. The block receives and returns 197 rows, each 192 features wide.
notes:
Have we finished the entire block after the attention residual?
We have reached U, the midpoint. Open the MLP branch next. E¹ names the output of block 1; it is not a power. Both branches update CLS and every patch row.

title: Open the MLP: 192 inputs, 768 hidden units, 192 outputs
caption: Each linear layer connects every input feature to every output unit. GELU transforms each hidden activation. Only a few neurons are drawn; dots omit the rest. The displayed numbers are measured values for this dog’s CLS row.
notes:
Does 768 mean patches, pixels, or hidden features here?
It is the number of hidden features for one row. GELU is the nonlinearity between the two learned linear layers. The MLP returns a 192-feature update; the residual addition follows.

title: Add the MLP update to finish block 1
caption: Keep the row produced by attention and add the MLP’s update. The result is this row’s output from block 1. Apply the same operation to all 197 rows. Their feature values change; their identities and width stay the same.
notes:
Do we add the MLP update to E or to U?
Add it to U, the result of the attention residual. There are two successive residual additions in the block. Its final output includes both updates.

title: Pass the complete output of block 1 into block 2
caption: The entire output matrix continues to the next block: CLS and all 196 patch rows. Block 2 has its own attention and MLP weights. It applies the same sequence of operations to the feature values produced by block 1.
notes:
Which rows do we keep, and which block processes them next?
Keep every row. Follow the straight arrow into a distinct block 2. There is no return to block 1, no repeated patchification, and no new CLS token.

title: What changes as the rows move through the blocks?
caption: Each block recomputes queries, keys, values, attention weights and MLP activations from its input. Its learned parameters stay fixed during this forward pass. The next block uses a different parameter set. Matrix dimensions and row identities stay the same.
notes:
Are we changing the weights or the feature values when we run this dog forward?
The feature values change. The blocks already have their own stored weights, which stay fixed during inference. Training later computes gradients and the optimizer updates those stored parameters.

title: Continue through the stack, then classify the image
caption: Pass the updated features through blocks 1 to 12 in order. The architecture repeats, with separate learned parameters in each block. After block 12 and final normalization, read CLS and calculate one set of class scores for this image.
notes:
What does “12 blocks” repeat, and when do we make a prediction?
The attention-plus-MLP architecture repeats. A different block processes each successive representation. All rows continue through the stack; one classifier reads the final CLS.

title: Select CLS from the final feature matrix
caption: After block 12, all 197 rows are still present. Final LayerNorm keeps the same shape. Select the highlighted CLS row: one image summary with 192 features. Its values now reflect information gathered from this dog’s patches.
notes:
Which part of the 197 × 192 matrix enters the classifier?
Extract the entire first row, all 192 features. This CLS is the result after the blocks and final normalization, not the initial learned CLS parameter. We do not average the rows in this model.

title: Open the classifier: 192 features become 1,000 scores
caption: Every class has one output neuron connected to all 192 CLS features. Each neuron uses its own learned weights and bias to produce a score. Only three of the 1,000 class neurons are drawn. Their scores are measured.
notes:
Does one feature correspond to one class, or does every class read the whole summary?
Each class reads all 192 features with its own weighted sum. This class head is a single affine layer. It has no hidden layer or GELU; softmax converts its scores to probabilities next.

title: One class score is a weighted sum plus a bias
caption: Multiply each CLS feature by this class’s learned weight. Sum all 192 products and add its bias. For this dog, the Newfoundland neuron produces 15.4763. Every other class performs the same calculation with its own weights and bias.
notes:
What makes the Newfoundland score different from the Tibetan mastiff score?
They read the same image summary but use different learned weights and biases. The 190 omitted products still contribute. Keep the score separate from its later probability.

title: Turn all 1,000 scores into class probabilities
caption: Exponentiate each score and divide by the sum over all 1,000 classes. Newfoundland receives 95.73% probability. The displayed classes are only three alternatives; the remaining 997 also enter the denominator. Choose the class with the largest probability.
notes:
Would softmax over only these three displayed scores give the same answer?
No. All 1,000 scores contribute to the denominator. The remaining probability mass is shown explicitly. Attention softmax normalized over source rows; this softmax normalizes over image classes.

title: The same dog now has its final prediction
caption: The classifier reads the final CLS, scores 1,000 labels, and selects Newfoundland as the most probable class. Its probability for this photograph is 95.73%. We have completed one forward pass from pixels to an image prediction.
notes:
Did each patch predict its own label, or did the model make one image prediction?
The final CLS summarizes the contextual features for this one image. One class head reads that summary. The 95.73% is a model probability for this photograph, not an accuracy measurement.

title: Section 4 · Calculate attention with four patches
caption: Switch explicitly to a four-patch worksheet with chosen weights. Work out the operations that the real model performed at a larger scale.
notes:
Can we calculate an attention message ourselves?
Pause at the section question. Connect the previous result to the three steps, then advance to the concrete example.

title: A smaller task: classify the arrangement
caption: Now switch to a tiny grayscale image so we can calculate every step. Its label describes the arrangement of the filled patches.
notes:
What should the labels be for these two arrangements?
State the new worksheet task before revealing either label. Count four patches in each image: two filled and two empty.

title: Would just counting the patches solve it?
caption: The pieces tell us what is present. Their locations tell us how those pieces are arranged. Our worksheet label depends on that arrangement.
notes:
Which label can you choose if I only tell you “two filled, two empty”?
Count the pieces, then refer back to the two layouts. The same count is compatible with both answers.

title: Flatten P1 into four inputs
caption: The same four grayscale pixels become four input numbers. Flattening rearranges them; it has no weights or biases.
notes:
Which input comes from the bottom-left pixel?
Trace top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right. Each pixel supplies one grayscale value in this worksheet.

title: Compute the first coordinate with one neuron
caption: Four inputs, four weights of ¼, and one bias of 0 produce ink = 1. This projection applies no activation after the weighted sum.
notes:
What does this neuron output when all four pixels are 1?
Follow each weighted edge into the sum, then add the separate bias. Reveal the output. This is one of the layer’s four output neurons.

title: The same projection: matrix, neurons, then biases
caption: First multiply inputs by connection weights and sum at each neuron: [1, 0, 0, 0]. Then add one bias per output: [0, 0, 0, 1]. The fourth output is 0 + 1 = 1.
notes:
Why does output 4 become 1 when its four connection weights are zero?
Match each W column to one neuron’s incoming weights. Reveal the weighted sums, then the four biases, then the outputs. Output 4 adds its bias of 1 to a zero sum. This is one nn.Linear(4,4) layer with no activation. Reuse it for every patch.

title: Project all four patches of the first image
caption: The 16 grayscale pixels form four patches. Each patch supplies four inputs to the same layer and gets four output features. Even an empty patch produces [0, 0, 0, 1] because of the bias.
notes:
Are four output features describing one patch or the whole image?
One patch. Match each coloured 2×2 region to its input row and output row. There are four output rows. Add the same bias to each row; no activation follows.

title: Project the second image with the same layer
caption: Change the image from “Across the top” to “Down the left”. P2 and P3 exchange their pixel rows and content rows. The layer uses exactly the same weights and biases for both images.
notes:
Which output rows change when the filled patches move to the left?
P2 changes to [0,0,0,1]; P3 changes to [1,0,0,1]. P1 and P4 stay the same. Position has not been added yet. Keep row order: top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right.

title: Would the mean pixel value tell these patches apart?
caption: A patch can have the same average and a different pattern.
notes:
Which patch has a horizontal edge? Which has a vertical edge?
Count two ones in each, then compare their positions.

title: Could two projection columns keep that difference?
caption: Each column combines the same pixels in a different way.
notes:
What does the first column subtract from what?
Calculate the top-edge patch against each column, then try the left-edge patch.

title: We have several patch rows. Where does the answer go?
caption: The classification token (CLS) is an extra learned row used to collect information for the image label.
notes:
We have many contextual patch rows. How could we produce one image label?
Point to the extra row and spell out classification token. It gathers information before the classifier produces a label.

title: Where does CLS come from?
caption: CLS is an extra learned input vector with the same width as a patch row.
notes:
Which image pixels were used to create CLS?
Point to the separate parameter, then count five rows entering attention.

title: These patches look the same. How do we tell them apart?
caption: Their content rows match. Their positions do not.
notes:
Which coordinate changes for the top-right patch?
Keep the filled patch content fixed and add its column location.

title: Give each patch a location vector
caption: Two patches can look alike and still come from different places.
notes:
Which entries record the row and column here?
Read each location from the small image grid.

title: Add content and location, coordinate by coordinate
caption: These five rows form E, the input to our attention calculation.
notes:
What distinguishes P1 from P2 now?
Compare the two filled patches after adding positions.

title: Can the top-left patch read the bottom-right?
caption: We already have the whole image when we predict its label, so all patches can read one another.
notes:
What future information would leak from another patch in this task?
Compare a lower-triangular next-token mask with all-to-all image attention.

title: Why did our text predictor hide later tokens?
caption: A causal mask prevents the model from reading the answer it is meant to predict.
notes:
Would seeing the next training token make prediction unfairly easy?
Read one matrix row as a receiver and its permitted source columns.

title: Why do we make three versions of each row?
caption: Matching a source and reading its information are two different jobs.
notes:
Which two vectors decide the weight, and which vector gets multiplied by it?
Recall bank’s request and river’s information from Part II. Keep the photo crop visible.

title: Which part of the picture could help this dark crop?
caption: Imagine borrowing nearby face evidence to interpret a patch of dark fur.
notes:
Would the face crop or the branches help more with this particular ambiguity?
Keep the receiver fixed and point to two possible sources.

title: Each row makes a query, a key and a value
caption: Q and K decide the weights. V supplies the message that gets weighted.
notes:
Can the same patch receive information and also send information?
Trace all three projections from the same row.

title: How could the face crop get more weight?
caption: Exponentiate the two scores: 3 and 1. Their shares are ¾ and ¼.
notes:
Where does the factor 3 come from?
Multiply q by each key, then normalize the two exponentials.

title: What do we receive after choosing those weights?
caption: Multiply each source’s value by its weight, then add the two vectors.
notes:
Does choosing the face with ¾ weight discard the other source?
Calculate both contributions before adding them.

title: Change only the keys. What happens?
caption: The values stay available, but their shares in the message change.
notes:
Which source now gets three times the weight of the other?
Swap the two keys and recompute the mixture.

title: Change only a value. What happens?
caption: The attention weights stay the same, but the received information changes.
notes:
Would an attention heatmap show this change?
Keep the two weights visible while doubling the first value coordinate.

title: Do we type a question into this classifier?
caption: No text prompt is needed. The image rows generate their own Q, K and V.
notes:
Where does the query come from if nobody types a question?
Follow the numerical projection from the input rows.

title: Which weights create the query, key and value?
caption: One input row; three separate learned projections. These worksheet weights are chosen for arithmetic.
notes:
What does each nonzero matrix entry copy or scale?
Follow the constant into Q, then ink and row into K and V.

title: Where does the CLS query [1,1] come from?
caption: Each query coordinate is a dot product with one column of W_Q.
notes:
Which input coordinate supplies both ones?
Use the W_Q columns shown on the previous slide and multiply all four terms.

title: How does P1 get the key [√2,0]?
caption: Head 1 keeps ink and row in its keys.
notes:
Would the constant 1 in the input affect this key?
Point to the zero in the last row of each key column.

title: Which features does this head compare?
caption: Part II again: the query and keys choose where to read.
notes:
What does multiplying this input by W_Q do?
Point to the fixed last coordinate supplying [1,1]. Then construct P1’s key.

title: Can we work out one score before filling the table?
caption: The head has two query/key coordinates, so d_k is 2.
notes:
Should the denominator use 2, 4 or 5 here?
Distinguish head width, embedding width and number of source rows.

title: What does softmax do when the scores tie?
caption: Equal scores get equal shares. Only score differences affect the shares.
notes:
Are two very negative scores less than 100% in total?
Compare the first and third rows, then explain the middle row using exponentials 1 and 3.

title: Repeat the dot product for every source
caption: Keep the query fixed. Only the source key changes.
notes:
Which of these keys give the same score?
Work down the five sources, including CLS.

title: Exponentiate the five scores
caption: Scores 0 and 1 become 1 and e.
notes:
Why are four exponentials equal?
Match each exponential to its score.

title: Divide by one shared sum
caption: The five source weights now add up to one.
notes:
What fraction belongs to CLS?
Divide its exponential 1 by the same sum used for every patch.

title: Where does the 0.229 beside P1 come from?
caption: Every source appears in the same denominator, including CLS.
notes:
What would go wrong if each patch used a different denominator?
Sum the five source contributions first, then divide one exponential by that sum.

title: Put each value beside its weight
caption: Keep a patch’s weight and value on the same row.
notes:
Which value belongs to the weight for P3?
Trace the source label across the table.

title: Multiply the value by its weight
caption: One scalar scales both coordinates of the source value.
notes:
Does the second coordinate get a different weight?
Multiply both entries before moving to the next row.

title: Add the contributions to get one message
caption: Add down each coordinate column.
notes:
How do five source rows become a two-number message?
Sum each coordinate separately, then reveal the result.

title: Can an empty patch still send something?
caption: An empty patch still has a position, and its value can carry that information.
notes:
Which coordinate receives the contribution from P3?
Multiply both coordinates by the same weight; keep the zero visible.

title: Do equal weights send equal information?
caption: Compare the values beside the weights. They tell us what each patch sends.
notes:
What do these two patches contribute to the ink coordinate?
Multiply both coordinates and compare the resulting messages.

title: What if the query cared only about ink?
caption: Change the query and keep the sources fixed. The mixture changes.
notes:
Which filled patches should get more weight now?
Set the second query coordinate to zero, then recompute all five scores.

title: Section 5 · More than one attention head
caption: Keep the same input rows. Change the head’s learned projections and follow the second calculation.
notes:
What could a second head tell us?
Pause at the section question. Connect the previous result to the three steps, then advance to the concrete example.

title: What might different heads look for in this photograph?
caption: Different heads can learn different matching patterns and different messages. Local texture, relationships between parts and wider context are possible intuitions. These are hypotheses, not measured head labels.
notes:
Could one mixture preserve all the different clues that matter for this image?
Connect to coat reading colour and material in Part III. Each visual role is a possible interpretation, not a hand-written rule or guaranteed specialization.

title: Three heads read the same rows in three learned ways
caption: Each head produces its own attention matrix and message. Join the messages, then mix them with the output projection. The number of heads is independent of the number of image classes.
notes:
Would a two-class dog/cat task require exactly two heads?
No. Compare three 64-wide heads with two class scores. Keep head count, feature width and class count separate.

title: Would a second way of reading the image help?
caption: As with colour and material in the coat example, we can keep two different messages.
notes:
What two kinds of information might help distinguish these layouts?
Point to row and column. Keep the same patches on both sides.

title: Head 2 compares ink and column
caption: The same input rows now pass through a different key projection.
notes:
Which patch has both ink and column equal to 1?
Point to P2 before calculating its score.

title: Give Head 2 its own softmax
caption: Each head divides by its own sum of exponentials.
notes:
Can we reuse Head 1’s denominator here?
Compare the score lists before normalizing.

title: What information does Head 2 send?
caption: Its values carry ink and column.
notes:
Which value coordinate changed from Head 1?
Keep the same source labels while comparing value definitions.

title: Calculate each Head 2 contribution
caption: Use Head 2’s weight and Head 2’s value from the same source.
notes:
Which source contributes most to the ink coordinate?
Compute P2’s product, then compare the other sources.

title: Add Head 2’s contributions
caption: We now have a second two-number message.
notes:
Are the two heads’ messages equal?
Compare the sums with Head 1’s result.

title: Do the patch rows get updated too?
caption: Yes. Here every query is [1,1], so the messages match. Each row still has its own starting vector.
notes:
Do identical messages imply identical updated rows?
Compare the queries, then remind students that each residual starts from a different E row.

title: Keep both messages by putting them side by side
caption: Concatenation gives us four numbers; it does not average the heads.
notes:
What would we lose by averaging these two rows immediately?
Follow all four coordinates into the joined row.

title: Use W_O to make the first update coordinate
caption: The first column subtracts Head 2’s ink value from Head 1’s.
notes:
Which two entries of W_O make that subtraction?
Trace the +1 and −1 from the joined row.

title: Collect all four output coordinates
caption: The update has the same width as the row we will add it to.
notes:
Why do we need four update coordinates?
Match the update width to E before moving to the residual.

title: What do the other columns of W_O produce?
caption: Use the same joined row for every output coordinate.
notes:
Which column adds information from both heads?
Read W_O column by column, matching these results to the full update vector.

title: Section 6 · From messages to an image label
caption: Follow the summary row through the classifier and loss. Then compare it with averaging the patch rows.
notes:
How do those messages become a prediction?
Pause at the section question. Connect the previous result to the three steps, then advance to the concrete example.

title: What if attention sent a zero message?
caption: The residual gives the next block a direct path from the starting row.
notes:
Would the original row disappear if the attention output were zero?
Add coordinate by coordinate, then connect this to the nonzero update in our main example.

title: Add the message to the starting CLS row
caption: Only the last starting coordinate is nonzero in this example.
notes:
Which coordinate changes because the original CLS contains a 1?
Add the two rows one coordinate at a time.

title: Use the updated CLS row to score the two labels
caption: The class matrix maps four coordinates to two scores.
notes:
Why does a negative first coordinate favour Across here?
Apply −4 and +4 to that same coordinate.

title: We used softmax twice. What changed?
caption: The formula is the same. The alternatives being compared are different.
notes:
Should the five attention weights sum with the two class probabilities?
Circle the alternatives separately. Each softmax has its own denominator.

title: Turn the class scores into probabilities
caption: The alternatives here are Across and Down.
notes:
Which two exponentials belong in this denominator?
Normalize over the two labels, then read the bars.

title: Use the known label to calculate the loss
caption: For this image, the correct label is Across the top.
notes:
Which probability belongs inside the logarithm?
Keep the image and correct label visible while calculating the loss.

title: How much does a confident wrong answer cost?
caption: Training lowers the loss by increasing the probability of the known label.
notes:
Which prediction should receive the largest penalty?
Compare all three cases using the same correct label.

title: Use the gradient to change the class bias
caption: Subtract half the gradient from the two bias values.
notes:
Why does the correct class bias increase?
Read the sign of p minus the one-hot target.

title: Run the prediction again after that update
caption: The correct-class probability rises and its loss falls on this example.
notes:
Did changing the bias alter the image or the attention weights?
Keep the frozen worksheet separate from the two bias values we changed.

title: Move the patches. Does the answer change?
caption: Make a prediction, change the arrangement, then turn positions off.
notes:
Will the class probabilities change if we permute patches without position information?
Take a prediction, choose Down the left, then turn positions off.

title: Who teaches CLS what information to collect?
caption: The image-classification loss sends gradients through the classifier and the attention blocks.
notes:
Is there a separate label telling CLS which patch to read?
Trace the loss backward through the computational path.

title: Could we classify the image without CLS?
caption: Averaging the final patch rows gives one image summary. This is called mean pooling.
notes:
Can you calculate the two coordinates of the mean?
Add each column and divide by the number of patch rows.

title: So why use CLS in our ViT?
caption: It gives the model a dedicated row whose final representation is trained for the image label.
notes:
What must both of these paths produce before the class head?
Follow each route to one fixed-width vector.

title: Run the same computation backward from the label loss
caption: The forward pass made a prediction. The backward pass measures how each parameter influenced its loss. Use the same four-patch worksheet and the same known label: Across the top.
notes:
Does backward itself change any learned weight?
No. It computes derivatives. The later optimizer step uses those derivatives to change parameters. The worksheet omits LayerNorm and MLP; we restore them in the full-block diagram.

title: First ask how the two class scores should change
caption: For softmax followed by cross-entropy, the score gradient is p − y. A negative gradient means increasing that score would locally reduce this example’s loss.
notes:
Why is the gradient of the correct score negative?
A parameter update subtracts its gradient. Separate a derivative from the later update. Both class scores receive a signal.

title: The class loss sends a gradient into the final CLS row
caption: Each score contributes through its classifier weight. Add those contributions to find the gradient of the CLS representation. The other coordinates have zero gradients here because our chosen classifier ignores them.
notes:
Can an image label train the summary without a separate CLS target?
Follow the two score branches backward into the same coordinate. The image label already supplies the learning signal.

title: The residual and both heads receive the learning signal
caption: Our output projection adds Head 1’s first coordinate and subtracts Head 2’s. Backpropagation follows those signs. The residual also passes a gradient directly to the starting CLS row.
notes:
Why does Head 2 receive the opposite sign?
Point to the minus sign in the forward expression. Reverse the existing W_O operation; do not invent an independent target for either head.

title: Learning can change what a source sends and how much we read
caption: For message Σⱼ aⱼvⱼ, the value gradient is aⱼ times the incoming gradient. The attention-weight gradient is its dot product with vⱼ. The loss reaches source patches through both routes.
notes:
Do patch values receive gradients even though the classifier reads only CLS?
Calculate one P1 product. Then notice the gradients in patch rows that have no direct classification readout.

title: The source scores compete for attention weight
caption: Softmax couples the source weights: increasing one score changes all weights. Subtract the weighted mean gradient, then multiply by each source weight to get the score gradients.
notes:
Why can we not update every attention weight independently?
They must stay normalized. The score gradients sum to zero; adding the same constant to every score leaves softmax unchanged.

title: Follow the score gradients into queries and keys
caption: Each dot product depends on both its query and its key. Reverse those products, then reverse the shared linear projections. The loss can improve which sources match the receiver.
notes:
What teaches a head which visual clues are useful?
The class loss trains the projections through this chain. No person labels a head as the eye head or fur head.

title: Use the gradient to change one query weight
caption: We update one query-projection weight with a small SGD step, then repeat the same forward pass. This hand calculation changes the attention mechanism itself and lowers this example’s loss.
notes:
Which quantity must be recomputed after the weight changes?
Q, scores, attention weights, messages, class scores and loss. This one-example improvement says nothing about held-out accuracy.

title: Every patch contributes to the same projection weights
caption: The patch projection is shared, so add its gradient contributions across patches. Position vectors and the starting CLS vector also receive gradients. The usual training step changes parameters, while the photograph stays fixed.
notes:
Do we now learn 196 separate patch projections?
No. Contributions accumulate into one parameter matrix. In a batch, contributions also accumulate across images before the optimizer step.

title: Section 7 · The complete Transformer block
caption: Put attention back inside the full block and follow what each operation changes.
notes:
What else belongs in the model we train?
Pause at the section question. Connect the previous result to the three steps, then advance to the concrete example.

title: Put the familiar attention inside a full block
caption: Attention mixes information across rows. The MLP transforms each row separately.
notes:
Which operation communicates between patches, and which works on one row at a time?
Point to attention, then the MLP; trace both residual paths.

title: Which operation lets one patch borrow from another?
caption: Attention mixes source value rows using weights chosen for the receiver.
notes:
Which arrows cross from one patch to another?
Point to several source rows contributing to one destination row.

title: What does the MLP change?
caption: The MLP combines coordinates within each row and applies a nonlinearity.
notes:
Does this MLP directly read a neighbouring patch row?
Keep one row highlighted as it passes through the two linear layers.

title: What average are we subtracting?
caption: LayerNorm works across the coordinates of this one row.
notes:
Are the other patches included in this mean?
Keep the four coordinates together and calculate their mean.

title: How spread out is the centered row?
caption: Square the deviations, take their mean, then take the square root.
notes:
Why do positive and negative deviations not cancel here?
Square each deviation before averaging. Mention epsilon on the next slide.

title: What does LayerNorm do to one row?
caption: Normalize across the coordinates of each token, independently of other tokens.
notes:
Which numbers participate in the mean and variance?
Use the four coordinates of one row; do not average across patches or the batch.

title: How does the MLP make a wider row?
caption: The first linear layer mixes coordinates within the same token.
notes:
Where does the zero in the hidden row come from?
Compute 1×1 + (−1)×1 using the third column.

title: Apply GELU to each hidden coordinate
caption: GELU(1) is about 0.841, and GELU(−1) is about −0.159.
notes:
Does GELU send every negative input to zero?
Compare the two signs using these actual values.

title: How does the MLP return to the original width?
caption: The second linear layer produces an update that can be added to the starting row.
notes:
Why must the output width be two in this example?
Match its width to the residual row [1,−1].

title: Add the MLP message to the starting row
caption: Both vectors have width two, so we can add them coordinate by coordinate.
notes:
Where does the 1.841 come from?
Add 1 and 0.841, then repeat for the second coordinate.

title: What does the next block get to see?
caption: The next block starts from rows that have already read the image.
notes:
Has the query in block two already seen other patches indirectly?
Trace the first residual update into the next block’s query projection.

title: The full block sends gradients through both residual branches
